subject.title: Idea 61: Since there’s no help, come let us kiss and part
subject.author: Michael Drayton
subject.text:
Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part.
Nay, I have done, you get no more of me;
And I am glad, yea glad with all my heart,
That thus so cleanly I myself can free.
Shake hands for ever, cancel all our vows,
And when we meet at any time again,
Be it not seen in either of our brows
That we one jot of former love retain.
Now at the last gasp of Love's latest breath,
When, his pulse failing, Passion speechless lies;
When Faith is kneeling by his bed of death,
And Innocence is closing up his eyes-
Now, if thou wouldst, when all have given him over,
From death to life thou might'st him yet recover!

title: A Young Man's Breakup Poem, Written at Fifty-Six
standfirst: "Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part" reads like a poet cutting a fresh wound loose in real time. Michael Drayton actually added it to his sonnet sequence a quarter of a century after he started it, about a woman who had belonged to someone else for over twenty years — and he was still writing to her memory when he died.

sections.heading: A Very Fresh-Sounding Goodbye
sections.body:
Everything about the opening quatrain sounds like it was written in the room where the breakup happened. "Nay, I have done, you get no more of me" has the clipped, overcorrecting rhythm of someone talking themselves out of a relationship they are still in — the repeated *glad*, twice in one line, doing exactly the work overinsistence always does in speech. It is, by general consent, the best-remembered sonnet Michael Drayton ever wrote, and it reads as the record of a single bad night.

It was not. Drayton's sonnet sequence *Idea* — addressed throughout to one woman under one invented name — had already been in print, and in revision, for twenty-five years by the time this poem entered it. He was not a young man discovering heartbreak. He was in his mid-fifties, closing out a project he had been carrying since he was thirty.

sections.heading: Twenty-Five Years Into the Same Sequence
sections.body:
Drayton published the sequence first as *Ideas Mirrour* in 1594, fifty-one sonnets addressed to "Idea." He kept revising it for the rest of his working life, reprinting it under the shorter title *Idea* in 1599, 1600, 1605 and finally 1619 — each pass rewriting, reordering, cutting and adding poems, until only twenty of the original fifty-one survived unaltered. "Since there's no help" is not one of the twenty. The scholarly edition of the sequence records that it "appears for the first time" in that last 1619 printing, calling it, in the same breath, a poem that carries "the tragedy of a whole life."

That is not a figure of speech about the poem's feeling. It is a fact about its date. Whatever this sonnet is a goodbye to, it was written by a man near sixty summing up something, not by one working out a fresh wound in real time.

sections.heading: The Page Who Grew Up Alongside Idea
sections.body:
Drayton's connection to the woman behind "Idea" went back further than the sonnets themselves. Around 1573, at about ten years old, he entered the household of Sir Henry Goodere as a page, sharing the family's tutors alongside Goodere's children — among them his daughter Anne, then a small child herself. Drayton later called her his "deerest Love," and early readers of *Idea* had little doubt she was its subject, dressed up under a name borrowed from Neoplatonic philosophy rather than her own.

So the relationship the 1619 sonnet supposedly ends had been running, in one form or another, for roughly forty-six years by the time the poem appeared — nearly the whole of Drayton's adult life, and most of Anne's.

sections.heading: Married to Someone Else Since the 1590s
sections.body:
The other detail the poem leaves out: Anne Goodere had married someone else decades earlier. She became the wife of Henry Rainsford of Clifford Chambers, in Warwickshire, in the mid-1590s — not long after *Ideas Mirrour* first appeared — and Drayton did not disappear from her life when she did. A biography of his years at Clifford Chambers describes bonds of "loyal service, tenderest affection and devoted and enduring friendship" stretching across three generations of the Goodere and Rainsford families, long after any hope of marrying Anne himself had passed.

Read against that, "come let us kiss and part" is not a man leaving a relationship. It is a man, decades into an arrangement that was never going to become one, writing the breakup he never actually got to have.

sections.heading: The Trick in the Last Six Lines
sections.body:
The craft carries the reversal. Three quatrains of brisk, businesslike renunciation — hands shaken, vows cancelled, no trace of former love to be seen on either brow — give way in the sestet to a small deathbed drama. Love lies on his last gasp; Passion is speechless; "Faith is kneeling by his bed of death, / And Innocence is closing up his eyes." Then, in the final couplet, the whole performance of composure collapses: *now, if thou wouldst* — right now, at the actual last second — she could still bring him back from the dead.

It is a Shakespearean sonnet in form, three quatrains and a couplet in iambic pentameter, and it uses that form's hinge exactly as intended: everything the octave and the third quatrain build up gets undone in two lines. The poet who spent twelve lines insisting he is glad is revealed, at the very end, to still be waiting by the door.

sections.heading: He Never Actually Managed the Clean Break
sections.body:
Drayton did not stop there, either. Accounts of his final years record that he was still writing unpublished verses to Anne's memory close to his own death in December 1631 — the goodbye of 1619 turning out to be no more final than any of the vows he had cancelled at the start of the poem. He was buried in Poets' Corner at Westminster Abbey, with a monument paid for by the Countess of Dorset and memorial verses attributed to his friend Ben Jonson, in the same stretch of the Abbey that would later gather up most of English poetry's dead.

The most convincing clean break in Elizabethan love poetry, in other words, was written by a man who spent the better part of sixty years failing to manage one. That may be exactly why it still reads as true: the confidence of "you get no more of me" is the sound of someone who has said it, unsuccessfully, before.
